venue_now: arXiv 2602.11570v1, 12 Feb 2026 (p.1); the text names no venue. The bibliography's ACL 2026 comes from the search catalogue (candidates/process_supervision.json); see notes/arxiv_abs_check.json for the arXiv page's comments. what_it_is: A benchmark of verifiers, not of solvers: 2,530 (solution, label) samples on which a verifier must decide whether a model's response is correct in both outcome and derivation (p.1-2, p.5-6). Problems come from a pool of over 7M undergraduate and graduate textbook and final-exam problems, filtered by GPT-OSS-120B for verifiability and by Gemini-3-Pro, GPT-5 and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 for answer correctness (p.4); several LRMs each write one response per problem, and only responses on which a proxy verifier (GPT-OSS-120B, eight trials) is inconsistent are kept (p.5). Eighteen domain experts give each response two binary labels, outcome correct and overall correct (sound derivation that reaches the answer); the overall label is the metric (p.2, p.5-6). The paper also uses the benchmark to select verifiers for process-aware RLVR (p.8-10).
domain: college-level STEM. Figure 3 (p.5, an image in the PDF) gives mathematics 36%, chemistry 28%, biology 19% and engineering 18% (mechanical/aerospace, electrical/computing, civil/materials, systems/robotics; chemistry also lists chemical engineering); the results table reports mathematics, physics, chemistry and biology, with no engineering column (p.6); section 3.1 says the pool spans mathematics, physics, chemistry and engineering (p.4)
size: 2,530 expert-labelled responses (p.1-2); about 34 verifiers evaluated (Table 1, p.6)
source_of_items: textbooks and university final exams (p.4); responses generated by LRMs (p.5)
has_gold_traces: no: the reference is a final answer, 'typically a final value or option without reasoning steps' (p.4)
evaluation: verifier accuracy against two binary expert labels per response (outcome; overall process-outcome consistency), plus F1 on the overall label (p.5-7); 16.98% of responses in an initial annotation were 'lucky guesses', correct answers from flawed derivations (p.2); verifiers score 4.66% to 45.92% on that subset (Table 4, p.15)
human_validation: 18 domain experts label every sample (p.2, p.5); no inter-annotator agreement is reported (no kappa or agreement figure anywhere in the text). The experts' labels are the benchmark's ground truth; they are per response, not per step

engtrace_use.sentence: Beyond mathematics, PRIME tests whether verifiers catch answers that the reasoning does not support, in mathematics and engineering [@wang2026prime], and ChemCoTBench-V2 checks chemistry steps with deterministic rules [@guo2026chemcotbenchv2].
engtrace_use.explanation: The task is right: the overall label is valid only if the reasoning is sound and correctly derives the answer, so verifiers must reject correct answers reached by flawed derivations (p.5-6). 'In mathematics and engineering' follows the title but not the data: engineering is 18% of the benchmark by Figure 3 (p.5), chemistry and biology together 47%, and the results table has no engineering column (p.6). 'Beyond mathematics' is also loose, since mathematics is the largest share (36%). Better: college-level STEM, engineering included.

suggested_wording: PRIME tests whether verifiers reject correct answers reached by flawed derivations in college-level science and engineering problems, against experts' labels for each solution [@wang2026prime].
facts_to_cite: problems from textbooks and university final exams spanning mathematics, physics, chemistry and engineering (p.4)
each response gets an outcome label and an overall (process-outcome consistency) label; the overall label is the metric (p.5-6)
16.98% of responses were 'lucky guesses': correct outcome, flawed derivation (p.2)
verifiers reach 4.66% to 45.92% on the lucky-guess subset (Table 4, p.15)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: the target failure (a correct answer from flawed reasoning); engineering content (18%); expert labels used to measure evaluators. Lacks: generated instances (static textbook problems); gold traces (final answers only, p.4); any deterministic check of intermediate values; step-level labels (two binary labels per response, p.5); agreement statistics for its experts. The positioning claim holds against it. It is a meta-evaluation benchmark, not a reasoning benchmark, so it does not belong in Table A, whose columns describe benchmarks of solvers.
notes: (1) The paper contradicts itself on its composition: Figure 3 has engineering (18%) and no physics; Table 1 has physics and no engineering (p.5-6). (2) Its rule-based verifier (Math-Verify) is given an answer extracted by GPT-OSS-120B (p.7), and its case study shows a rule-based verifier rejecting '4pi' against '4 pi' (p.15), which supports the format-failure point v3 makes with huang2026verifierrobustness. (3) The difficulty filter keeps only responses a proxy verifier is unsure about (p.5), so scores are not population rates.
